prize_parts.citation: for the theoretical prediction of the quantum spin Hall state and its first experimental observation, which established topological insulators as a new class of quantum matter

statement.case_for: Having read the other seven openings, I move B013 ahead of my own first choice B008. Seven of eight members put it in their top three, and the reason is not just numbers: it is the one candidate where the theory-experiment chain is complete and clean. Kane and Mele predicted a Z2 quantum spin Hall state from spin-orbit coupling and time-reversal symmetry, and Molenkamp's group then found the protected edge channels in HgTe wells, with quantised conductance, in 2007. That is the nature-gives-the-clue pattern I care about, because the prediction could have failed and did not. Many independent groups and materials (transport, ARPES) have confirmed it for almost two decades, so the maturity question is closed. It is also a discovery with a clear one-sentence statement and conceptual reach into photonics, cold atoms and classification of matter.
statement.case_against: The allocation is genuinely unresolved. Three names cannot cover Kane, Mele, Molenkamp and Hasan, and the Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang proposal that actually told Molenkamp where to look is outside the credited set, with Zhang now deceased. The Nobel Foundation cannot give credit to the dead, so the committee would be handing out a prize in which a decisive step goes unrecognised. There is also a thematic worry: the 2016 prize already covered topological phases, so some will see this as a second helping. I think the physics is distinct (symmetry-protected band topology in real materials rather than topological phase transitions in model systems), but the citation has to say so clearly. Finally, B008 remains for me the purest example of a clue from nature, and its one-name credit is a serious weakness in the other direction.

responses.point: Eriksson ranks B013 first for the closure between first-principles band structure and ARPES/transport, and would swap Mele for Hasan to cover theory, transport and 3D materials.
responses.response: I agree on the quality of the closure and it moves me toward B013. But I would keep Mele rather than Hasan. The Z2 invariant and the quantum spin Hall idea are the conceptual core, and Kane and Mele are a single theory contribution that cannot honestly be split. Hasan's 3D ARPES work is a strong second experimental strand, but a prize crediting two experimentalists and one theorist would leave the founding classification without its second author. If the committee wants 3D topological insulators recognised, that is a point for the citation text, not a reason to drop Mele.

responses.point: Pearce puts B008 first as the creation of neutrino astronomy as a working field, and notes that a single credited name probably should be broadened with pioneers or collaboration leaders who are not on the credited list.
responses.response: This is the point on which I am least comfortable with my own opening ranking. I agree the science is a real window on the sky, mature and confirmed in several channels. But we can only name Halzen, and as you say the pioneers of the technique (AMANDA, Baikal, ANTARES) and the collaboration leadership are outside the credit. A one-person IceCube prize would be fragile under outside scrutiny, which is why I now hold it as the alternative and not the lead. If colleagues think the committee can defend a single laureate here, it can be paired as a second part in a different configuration.

responses.point: Johansson ranks circuit QED first as the basis of present superconducting processors, reproduced by many laboratories, and sees the 2025 prize as making the recognition natural rather than premature.
responses.response: I would qualify that. The 2025 prize on macroscopic quantum tunnelling in superconducting circuits sits very close to this, and giving circuit QED directly afterwards risks reading as the same field twice, with Girvin and Devoret outside the credit. The engineering success is evident, but I want to see what is physically new that was not already in the 2025 citation. I would rather not rank it above a candidate whose novelty is clear.

responses.point: Mehlig ranks B013 first for a clean general mechanism, proposes two theorists plus the first experimentalist, and ranks anyons (B021) second with confirmation still maturing.
responses.response: I support your trio for B013 and our proposed names coincide. On B021 I am more cautious: fractional charge by shot noise is secure, but the anyonic braiding evidence is only a few years old and I would want more independent replication and an outside report before treating it as mature. Leinaas and Myrheim's 1977 idea is a fine example of theory waiting for nature, so I do not dismiss it, but I would not move it ahead of B013 now.

uncertainties: How to treat the Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang HgTe proposal, which falls outside the credited names and the three-person limit.
Whether the 2016 topological phase prize makes a second topology prize look repetitive, and how the citation should distinguish the two.
Whether a single-name IceCube prize for Halzen is defensible without the other detector pioneers, which I cannot verify from the provided files.
Whether anyonic braiding evidence (B021) will be independently replicated enough to change the ranking.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent from my profile for the shortlisted candidates. My PhD supervisor and frequent co-author are string and gravity theorists unconnected to these ballots; I note only that as Secretary I know the procedure for commissioning external reports and would want those for any candidate with a contested allocation.
